title: Shiva's lesson, heard from inside a fish
hookLine: Shiva teaches yoga to Parvati by the sea, a boy inside a fish listens in, and a line of teachers begins
carry: yoga passes from guru to student, back to shiva
tomorrow: can a single breath be a gift?

lines: A BOY IN A FISH OVERHEARS.
cards: On a lonely shore, the story goes, Shiva sat with Parvati and taught her the secret of yoga. But someone else was listening. Down in the water, a great fish had swallowed a boy, and from inside it he took in every word.

Shiva noticed, and blessed the listener, and the boy came out a master. He's remembered as Matsyendranath, lord of the fish. His student was Gorakhnath, and from the two of them comes a whole line of yogis.
Today: the line of teachers hatha yoga is handed down through, and why its own manual tells you to go slowly.

teach.h: GURU PARAMPARA: THE LINE OF TEACHERS
teach.b: That's a legend of the Nath yogis, and tellings differ; in some, the fish itself is the listener. The claim is the point: for the Naths and the hatha yogis, yoga isn't invented; it's received.
It comes down from Shiva, the first teacher, one student at a time.
That's guru parampara, the line of teachers, and it's one of Hinduism's deepest habits: knowledge that matters is passed hand to hand, from a guru to a student who is ready.
Hindus even keep a day for it, Guru Purnima, a full moon when students honor their teachers. The Hatha Yoga Pradipika shows the habit.

teach.h: HATHA, A STAIR TO THE STILL MIND
teach.b: Its author, Svatmarama, opens by bowing to Adinatha, the first lord, a name for Shiva, who taught hatha yoga as a stairway for anyone wanting to climb to the higher yoga of the still mind.
Then he names the line: Matsyendra, Gorakhnath and others. The body practice is a stair, not the summit. And what's handed down is handed down carefully.
In paraphrase: as a lion, an elephant or a tiger is tamed little by little, so the breath; otherwise it harms the one who practices.
It lists what careless practice brings, cough and pain among them, and also promises that right practice ends every disease; no doctor would promise that, so leave that line on the page.

teach.h: KEEP THE GURU, LEAVE THE CURE-ALL
teach.b: Keep the guru and the slowness. That's why, in traditional yoga, you don't learn breath practice from a stranger's video. You learn it from a teacher, who learned it from one, back toward Shiva by the sea.

how: In hatha yoga lineages, breath practices are learned gradually from a teacher; the Hatha Yoga Pradipika opens by bowing to Shiva as the first teacher, and many Hindus honor their teachers on Guru Purnima.

games.q: you've overheard Shiva's yoga from inside a fish, like Matsyendra. what do you do with it?
o: post it for anyone to try tonight.
teach it, carefully, to a student who's ready.
games.why: that's the line of teachers: received, then passed on hand to hand. Matsyendra taught Gorakhnath, and the line goes on.

practice: Let the breath move on its own and watch its pace, the way a keeper watches a lion before ever reaching out a hand; if anything strains, back to ordinary breathing.

Then bring to mind one teacher who handed you something that mattered, and whoever taught them, and let one breath of thanks go back down that line. If you pray, you can bow inwardly to the guru, as many Hindus do before practice.

wordCard.voice: The breath again. In the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, breath is tamed little by little, like a lion, and learned in a line of teachers that begins with Shiva. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: teacher; the word also means heavy, weighty. in tradition, yoga comes down a line of gurus.

carryVoice: Your line: yoga passes from guru to student, back to Shiva. Slowly, and hand to hand. Rest well.

sources.ref: Hatha Yoga Pradipika 1.1 (bow to Adinatha, who taught hatha yoga as a stairway to raja yoga)

Hatha Yoga Pradipika 2.15 (as a lion, elephant or tiger is tamed gradually, so the breath; otherwise it harms the practitioner)
